syllabus.clause: array, hash, sorted-list and ternary-search-tree children; O(key length) lookup independent of n; the memory blow-up that drives every later design.

at.step: Array children: one slot per possible character, found in one step with no comparison at all — and, measured on this exact 21-word dictionary, 96.3 percent of those slots sit empty.

Three other ways to store the same children, each trading the array’s free lookup step for something smaller: a hash table keyed by character, a sorted list of children searched by binary search, or a ternary search tree — a tiny three-child structure built around comparing one character at a time.

A ternary search tree node holds exactly one character, a value, and three children: lo and hi compare against the same character position, equal advances to the next one — the array’s own one-step-per-character discipline, kept, with three references instead of 26 slots.

Every chapter before this one paid a cost that grew with n — the number of keys stored. A trie lookup pays for exactly the key's own length, L, and nothing else: each step consumes one character and moves to exactly one child.
Prove it

at.step: A trie stores characters in its nodes, not keys: each node has one child per possible next character, and walking from the root one character at a time either finds the string or proves it isn't there.
